questions.question: What are the pros and cons of using Redis versus PostgreSQL for session storage in a web application?
reference: Redis stores sessions in memory, giving sub-millisecond latency and high throughput
Redis has built-in TTL/expiry, natural for temporary session data
Redis costs grow with RAM and it is less durable by default (persistence is optional)
PostgreSQL persists to disk and offers ACID durability and data integrity
PostgreSQL is slower for high-velocity session reads/writes than an in-memory store
Running sessions in PostgreSQL can consolidate infrastructure and avoid a extra cache layer
A common conclusion: Redis for speed/transient data, PostgreSQL when durability/simplicity of one store matters

questions.question: What are the main differences between Docker containers and virtual machines?
reference: VMs virtualize hardware via a hypervisor; each VM runs its own full guest OS
Containers share the host OS kernel and isolate only the process (namespaces/cgroups)
Containers are lighter, start in seconds, and images are MBs rather than GBs
VMs provide stronger isolation; containers have higher density on one host
Containers package the app plus dependencies for consistent environments

questions.question: What is database connection pooling and why is it used?
reference: A pool reuses existing open connections instead of opening/closing one per request
Opening connections costs TCP handshake + authentication time
The pool caps the number of concurrent connections, protecting the database from overload
Common tools/libraries: PgBouncer, HikariCP, SQLAlchemy pool
Trade-offs: stale connections, pool size tuning, and settings shared across clients

questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem and how do you fix it?
reference: It happens when you fetch a list (1 query) then run a separate query per row (N queries)
Often caused by lazy loading in ORMs
Result: N+1 round trips and badly degraded performance
Fixes: JOINs, eager loading (includes/prefetch_related), or one batched query with IN
It is a performance/latency problem, not a correctness problem

questions.question: Compare REST and GraphQL. When would you choose each?
reference: REST uses multiple endpoints with fixed response shapes; GraphQL uses a single endpoint with client-specified queries
GraphQL avoids over-fetching/under-fetching when clients need varied data
REST responses cache easily (HTTP semantics); GraphQL caching is harder
GraphQL suits complex, deeply related data and many client types (e.g. mobile)
GraphQL adds complexity and risks like query-depth attacks; REST is simpler for straightforward CRUD

questions.question: What problem does a CDN solve, and what are its limitations?
reference: A CDN caches content at edge servers close to users, reducing latency
It offloads traffic and bandwidth from the origin server
Best for static assets (images, CSS, video, static files)
Limitation: dynamic or personalized content is harder to cache; cache invalidation is tricky
Limitation: it does not fix slow application code or database bottlenecks

questions.question: What is the TLS handshake and why does HTTPS need it?
reference: The handshake establishes an encrypted channel before data is sent
The server proves its identity with a certificate signed by a trusted CA
The parties authenticate and exchange/session keys to derive a shared symmetric key
It prevents eavesdropping and tampering of the traffic
HTTPS is simply HTTP carried over TLS

questions.question: When should you choose SQLite over PostgreSQL for production?
reference: SQLite is embedded/serverless: a single file, no database server process
Good fit for read-heavy, low-write, single-node, local/edge, or embedded apps
Limitation: effectively a single writer, so poor concurrent-write throughput
Limitation: no network access, so multiple hosts/servers cannot share it
PostgreSQL is the better choice for multi-user, multi-server, high-concurrency workloads

questions.question: What are the trade-offs between Kafka and RabbitMQ?
reference: Kafka is a distributed append-only log with high throughput and message retention/replay
Kafka suits event streaming, logs, and pipelines where consumers read at their own pace
RabbitMQ is a traditional broker with per-message acknowledgements and flexible routing
RabbitMQ suits task queues and low-latency message delivery
Kafka generally has higher throughput but more operational complexity

questions.question: What does Kubernetes provide that Docker Compose does not?
reference: Kubernetes orchestrates containers across multiple machines; Compose is single-host
Kubernetes self-heals: restarts/reschedules failed containers
Kubernetes supports rolling/zero-downtime deploys and autoscaling
Kubernetes provides service discovery and load balancing between services
Compose is simpler and fine for development/small deployments; Kubernetes adds significant complexity

questions.question: When is SQL a better choice than NoSQL, and vice versa?
reference: SQL fits structured/relational data with a stable schema and relations to join
SQL/relational databases give ACID transactions and strong consistency
NoSQL (document, key-value, column, graph) fits flexible or semi-structured schemas
NoSQL often scales horizontally across many machines more easily
Choice depends on query patterns, consistency needs, and scale — not a universal winner

questions.question: Why should HTTP APIs be idempotent? Give examples.
reference: Idempotent = performing the same request multiple times has the same effect as once
It makes retries safe after timeouts or network failures
GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; POST is not by default
Prevents duplicate side effects such as double-charging a card
Non-idempotent operations can use idempotency keys to deduplicate retries

questions.question: What are the main benefits and limitations of serverless functions?
reference: Benefits: no server management, automatic scaling, pay-per-invocation pricing
Provider handles availability/infrastructure maintenance
Limitation: cold starts add latency
Limitation: execution time limits and vendor lock-in
Limitation: stateless by design — state must live elsewhere (database/storage); debugging is harder

questions.question: How does DNS resolution work, step by step?
reference: The browser/OS checks its local DNS cache first
If uncached, a recursive resolver queries on the client's behalf
The resolver walks the hierarchy: root server, then TLD server, then the domain's authoritative nameserver
The answer (A/AAAA address, possibly via CNAME chain) is returned to the client
Results are cached with a TTL to avoid repeat lookups

questions.question: What are the pros and cons of WebSockets versus Server-Sent Events?
reference: WebSockets are full-duplex: both sides send messages over one persistent connection
SSE is one-way: server pushes events to the client over plain HTTP
SSE is simpler, auto-reconnects, and works through standard HTTP infrastructure, but is text-only
WebSockets fit bidirectional use cases (chat, gaming, live collaboration)
Both require managing connection lifecycle, and the choice depends on whether the client needs to send data

questions.question: What is Redis persistence, and why is it often limited or disabled?
reference: Redis persistence options: RDB point-in-time snapshots and AOF append-only log of writes
Persistence adds latency and background I/O overhead
When Redis is only a cache or disposable session store, data can be rebuilt, so durability is unneeded
Disabling or loosening persistence buys speed
It is a durability-versus-performance trade-off, not a universal setting
